figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.places: Born at Thagaste (Souk Ahras, Algeria); schooled at Madauros and Carthage; taught rhetoric at Carthage, Rome and Milan; converted at Milan (386); baptised by Ambrose (Easter 387); his mother died at Ostia; priest (391) then bishop (395/6) of Hippo Regius (Annaba, Algeria), where he died during the Vandal siege
figures.role: Rhetoric professor turned bishop; the most prolific Latin Father; author of the Confessions and the City of God; chief opponent of the Manichaeans, the Donatists and the Pelagians
figures.status_note: Saint and Doctor of the Church in the Catholic Church (feast 28 August); commemorated by Anglicans and Lutherans; in the Orthodox Church usually honoured as 'Blessed Augustine' and a saint, but many Orthodox writers reject parts of his teaching (original guilt, the filioque, his strong predestination). Cautions for a reader: he taught that unbaptised infants are condemned (with the mildest punishment), that hell is eternal, and he came to defend state force against the Donatist schismatics after first opposing it. He also changed his mind in public on several things and wrote a whole book (the Retractations) correcting his earlier works, so always check which Augustine is speaking: early or late.
figures.hook: As a boy of sixteen he stole a load of pears he did not even want and threw them to the pigs, and thirty years later he spent pages of his life story trying to work out why.

stories.story: At sixteen he and a gang of friends stripped a neighbour's pear tree late at night. The pears were not even good. They ate a few and threw the rest to the pigs, and the thrill was simply that it was forbidden. Writing in his forties, he treats this petty theft as the key to how sin works.
stories.source: Confessions, Book II, chapter 4 (9)

stories.story: To get to Rome he lied to his mother Monica. She followed him to the harbour at Carthage to stop him or go with him, so he told her he was only seeing off a friend, and sailed in the night while she prayed in a chapel. He wrote: 'And I lied to my mother — and such a mother!— and got away.'
stories.source: Confessions, Book V, chapter 8 (15)

stories.story: In a garden in Milan, weeping over his inability to give up his old life, he heard a child's voice from a neighbouring house chanting 'Take up and read; take up and read.' He opened Paul's letters at random, read Romans 13:13-14, and his hesitation ended.
stories.source: Confessions, Book VIII, chapter 12 (29)

stories.story: Before his conversion he sent away the woman he had lived with for about fifteen years, the mother of his son Adeodatus, because she stood in the way of a socially suitable marriage. He wrote that his heart 'was racked, and wounded, and bleeding', and that she went back to Africa vowing never to know another man.
stories.source: Confessions, Book VI, chapter 15 (25)

stories.story: Visiting Hippo as a layman, he was grabbed by the congregation in church and pushed forward to be ordained priest against his will. He wept openly. Some people thought he was crying from wounded pride at not being made bishop; he told his friends later that he wept because he foresaw the dangers of governing a church.
stories.source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 4 (tr. Weiskotten 1919); Augustine, Letter 21.2

stories.story: He had a couplet carved on his dining table: 'Who injures the name of an absent friend / May not at this table as guest attend.' When some fellow bishops started gossiping anyway, he told them that either the verses came off the table or he would get up and leave in the middle of the meal. Possidius says he was there when it happened.
stories.source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 22

stories.story: Armed Donatist 'Circumcellions' laid an ambush for him on the road. His guide took a wrong turn by mistake, and he arrived safely by another way, learning of the trap only later.
stories.source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 12

stories.story: Dying during the Vandal siege of Hippo, he had the short penitential psalms copied out and hung on the wall by his bed, read them, and wept continually. For his last ten days he asked that no one come in except the doctors and whoever brought food, so he could pray. He left no will, because he owned nothing.
stories.source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 31

stories.story: At Ostia, days before she died, his mother told him and his brother: 'Lay this body anywhere, let not the care for it trouble you at all. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.' He held back his tears at the funeral, then wept for her alone afterwards and wrote that no one should laugh at him for it.
stories.source: Confessions, Book IX, chapters 11-12 (27, 33)

stories.story: When the Vandals overran Africa, bishops asked whether they could flee. He answered that ministers may not abandon a flock that still needs them, and that it is the hireling who flees when he sees the wolf. He stayed in Hippo and died there during the siege.
stories.source: Letter 228 to Honoratus, quoted in full by Possidius, Life, chapter 30

temperament.trait: Quick to tears, and not ashamed of them
temperament.evidence: He wept at his ordination, wept for his mother and defended it in writing, and wept constantly over the psalms on his deathbed.
temperament.source: Possidius, Life, chapters 4 and 31; Confessions IX.12.33

temperament.trait: Hated gossip and could be stern about it
temperament.evidence: The table couplet against slandering absent friends, and his threat to leave the meal when fellow bishops ignored it: 'Both I and the others who were at the table experienced this.'

temperament.trait: Restlessly curious and easily distracted, and he knew it
temperament.evidence: He admits that a dog chasing a hare in a field, or 'a lizard catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into her nets', could pull his mind away from serious thought.

temperament.trait: A relentless self-examiner, a puzzle to himself
temperament.evidence: After his friend's death: 'I became a great puzzle to myself.' Of his reaction to church music: 'in whose sight I have become a puzzle to myself; and this is my infirmity.'

temperament.trait: Willing to change his mind in public
temperament.evidence: On using force against the Donatists: 'originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ... But this opinion of mine was overcome'. Late in life he wrote the Retractations, reviewing and correcting his own books one by one.

Jerome, stung by Augustine's unsolicited criticism, told him: 'you are challenging an old man, disturbing the peace of one who asks only to be allowed to be silent, and you seem to desire to display your learning.'

temperament.trait: Intensely social; could not live without friends
temperament.evidence: He lists what he loved in friends: to talk and joke together, to read good books together, to disagree without ill-humour, 'longing for the absent with impatience, and welcoming the coming with joy.' He always lived in community, first with friends, then with his clergy.

genuine_lines.quote: for You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Too late did I love You, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love You! For behold, You were within, and I without, and there did I seek You
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Give what You command, and command what You will.
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
genuine_lines.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare
genuine_lines.work: Homilies on the First Epistle of John
genuine_lines.translation: H. Browne, NPNF1 vol. 7 (1888), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Blessed be he who loves You, and his friend in You, and his enemy for Your sake.
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?
genuine_lines.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that you may understand
genuine_lines.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
genuine_lines.translation: John Gibb, NPNF1 vol. 7 (1888), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote:
Who injures the name of an absent friend
May not at this table as guest attend.
genuine_lines.work: Inscription on his dining table, recorded by Possidius, Life of Augustine
genuine_lines.translation: Herbert T. Weiskotten (Princeton, 1919)

misattributed.line: In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.
misattributed.truth: Not in Augustine. It comes from 17th-century Protestant irenic writing (Rupertus Meldenius, c. 1626; an earlier form in Marco Antonio de Dominis, 1617).

misattributed.line: Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.
misattributed.truth: Not in Augustine. The saying is traced to Gabor Hevenesi's Scintillae Ignatianae (1705), which attributes a version of it to Ignatius of Loyola.

misattributed.line: He who sings prays twice (Qui bene cantat bis orat).
misattributed.truth: No such sentence is found in Augustine's works. The nearest is a remark in his Exposition on Psalm 72(73) that one who sings praise does not only praise but praises gladly; the proverb grew from later paraphrase.

misattributed.line: The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page.
misattributed.truth: No source in Augustine; it appears only in modern quotation collections.

misattributed.line: Hope has two beautiful daughters; their names are Anger and Courage.
misattributed.truth: No source in Augustine has ever been produced.

misattributed.line: Love the sinner, hate the sin.
misattributed.truth: Not his wording. The closest genuine line is in his Rule for nuns, Letter 211.11: 'with due love for the persons and hatred of the sin' (Latin: cum dilectione hominum et odio vitiorum), said about correcting faults in a community.

opinions.position: Use pagan learning freely. Whatever is true in the philosophers, especially the Platonists, belongs to Christ and should be taken over, like Israel taking the Egyptians' gold.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning side (with Clement and Origen, against Tertullian's 'what has Athens to do with Jerusalem').
opinions.quote: if those who are called philosophers, and especially the Platonists, have said anything that is true and in harmony with our faith, we are not only not to shrink from it, but to claim it for our own use from those who have unlawful possession of it.
opinions.location: Book II, chapter 40 (60); compare II.18.28: 'wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master'
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, Christian or not, agree; a minority of Christians distrust secular philosophy and higher education. Among the Fathers it splits sharply.

opinions.position: Every lie is a sin, even one told to help or save someone. Better to say 'I will neither lie nor betray' and suffer, as Bishop Firmus of Thagaste did when soldiers demanded the man he was hiding.
opinions.side_note: The strictest side: no lie is ever permitted, even to protect life (against Jerome and those who defended 'useful' lies). He grades lies by harm but calls all of them sin.
opinions.quote: Nor are we to suppose that there is any lie that is not a sin, because it is sometimes possible, by telling a lie, to do service to another.
opinions.location: chapter 22 (headed 'A Lie is Not Allowable, Even to Save Another from Injury'); see also On Lying 23 for Firmus
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly divides people. Most would lie to hide a refugee from killers (the classic 'murderer at the door' case); a minority, including some Christians and Kantians, would not.

opinions.position: Only God is to be enjoyed for His own sake. Everything else, however good, is to be used on the way home to Him, like a traveller who must not fall in love with the road.
opinions.side_note: A careful middle position: creatures are good and may be used with pleasure, but resting in them for their own sake is a disorder.
opinions.quote: For to enjoy a thing is to rest with satisfaction in it for its own sake. To use, on the other hand, is to employ whatever means are at one's disposal to obtain what one desires, if it is a proper object of desire
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today think it is fine to enjoy good things (food, art, people) for their own sake; the idea that only God may be 'enjoyed' strikes many as austere. Believers split.

opinions.position: No foods are unclean and wine is allowed, but he fought daily against the pull of eating and drinking. The aim is moderation, not heroic fasting: 'the bridle of the throat' held between slack and tight.
opinions.side_note: Moderate side. Possidius records that his table was plain, with meat for guests and always wine, because 'every creature of God is good'.
opinions.quote: I strive daily against longing for food and drink. For it is not of such a nature as that I am able to resolve to cut it off once for all, and not touch it afterwards, as I was able to do with concubinage. The bridle of the throat, therefore, is to be held in the mean of slackness and tightness.
opinions.location: Book X, chapter 31 (47); Possidius, Life, chapter 22
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree with moderation; few today would call a normal appetite for food a daily moral battle.

opinions.position: He looked back on his love of the theatre as a sickness: people pay to feel grief at pretend sorrows they would never want in real life. As a bishop he no longer went to the circus, though a hunt glimpsed in a field could still grip him.
opinions.side_note: Against the shows (with Tertullian), though argued from his own experience rather than rules.
opinions.quote: Stage-plays also drew me away, full of representations of my miseries and of fuel to my fire. Why does man like to be made sad when viewing doleful and tragical scenes, which yet he himself would by no means suffer?
opinions.location: Book III, chapter 2 (2); compare X.35.57 and VI.8.13 (Alypius at the gladiators)
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today see films and plays as good or neutral; a minority of Christians share the worry about violent or sensual entertainment. The specific question 'why do we enjoy sad stories?' still divides.

opinions.position: Singing in church is good because it moves weaker souls to devotion. But when the tune moves him more than the words, he counts it a sin and would rather not have heard the singing.
opinions.side_note: Torn, but finally on the approving side, with a strong suspicion of beauty that outruns meaning.
opinions.quote: being inclined rather (though I pronounce no irrevocable opinion upon the subject) to approve of the use of singing in the church, that so by the delights of the ear the weaker minds may be stimulated to a devotional frame. Yet when it happens to me to be more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess myself to have sinned criminally
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone today approves of music in worship; the question whether a beautiful tune can distract from the words still splits worshippers (traditional versus contemporary, choirs versus congregational singing).

opinions.position: A Christian may fight a just war, but only for the sake of peace, keeping faith even with the enemy and fighting in the spirit of a peacemaker. Even a just war is a misery to be lamented. The real evils of war are not deaths but cruelty, love of violence and lust for power.
opinions.side_note: The founding voice of Christian just-war thinking (against the early pacifist strand of Tertullian and Origen).
opinions.quote: Peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity, and waged only that God may by it deliver men from the necessity and preserve them in peace. For peace is not sought in order to the kindling of war, but war is waged in order that peace may be obtained.
opinions.location: section 6; see also City of God XIX.7 and Reply to Faustus XXII.74
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians and most people today accept that some wars are just; pacifists (Mennonites, Quakers, some others) disagree.

opinions.position: He came to support imperial laws that pressured the Donatist schismatics back into the Catholic Church, because he saw whole towns, including his own, come back and be glad of it. He admits this reversed his earlier view that no one should be coerced.
opinions.side_note: CHANGE OF MIND: early Augustine held 'words only'; the later Augustine (from about 405) accepted state coercion ('compel them to come in', Letter 93, Letter 185). He always opposed the death penalty for heretics.
opinions.quote: For originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ, that we must act only by words, fight only by arguments, and prevail by force of reason, lest we should have those whom we knew as avowed heretics feigning themselves to be Catholics. But this opinion of mine was overcome not by the words of those who controverted it, but by the conclusive instances to which they could point.
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone today, Christian or not, rejects using the state to force religious belief; this is one-sided now. The underlying question (can pressure ever be good for someone?) still splits.

opinions.position: No one should covet leadership. Being a bishop is a work, not an honour, and whoever loves ruling more than doing good is no bishop. But if the burden is laid on you, love requires you to carry it.
opinions.side_note: Reluctant-acceptance side: do not seek office, do not refuse it when laid on you. He himself was ordained weeping (Possidius 4; Letter 21).
opinions.quote: So that he who loves to govern rather than to do good is no bishop.
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree leaders should serve rather than seek power; opinion splits on whether one should ever turn down a responsibility others press on you.

opinions.position: Neither pure contemplation nor pure activity. No one may enjoy quiet so much that he neglects his neighbour, nor be so busy that he never contemplates God. He himself once planned to flee to the desert and felt God forbid it.
opinions.side_note: Mixed-life side: community and service over solitary withdrawal.
opinions.quote: No man has a right to lead such a life of contemplation as to forget in his own ease the service due to his neighbor; nor has any man a right to be so immersed in active life as to neglect the contemplation of God.
opinions.location: Book XIX, chapter 19; compare Confessions X.43.70 ('meditated flight into the wilderness; but You forbade me')
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today favour a balance, so this is fairly one-sided now; the real split is between people drawn to retreat and quiet and people who find it selfish.

opinions.position: Weeping for the dead is human and not a sin to be ashamed of, though he held back his tears at his mother's funeral out of faith and then let them flow in private. Friendship lost in death taught him how dangerous it is to love a mortal as if he would never die.
opinions.side_note: Grieve, but with hope; he defends tears against those who would call them faithless.
opinions.quote: Read it who will, and interpret how he will; and if he finds me to have sinned in weeping for my mother during so small a part of an hour — that mother who was for a while dead to my eyes, who had for many years wept for me, that I might live in Your eyes — let him not laugh at me
opinions.location: Book IX, chapter 12 (33); compare IV.4.9 on his friend's death
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone today agrees that grieving openly is healthy; the Stoic ideal of dry eyes is out of favour. One-sided now.

opinions.position: Marriage is good not only for children but for the companionship of husband and wife itself, which lives on in old age when desire has faded.
opinions.side_note: Against those (Jovinian's opponents, Manichaeans) who belittled marriage; he defends it as a real good.
opinions.quote: And this seems not to me to be merely on account of the begetting of children, but also on account of the natural society itself in a difference of sex.
opinions.translation: C.L. Cornish, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost universally agreed today.

opinions.position: Marriage and a life of continence are both goods, but continence is the higher good.
opinions.side_note: The common patristic ranking; Jovinian, whom Jerome and Augustine answered, denied it.
opinions.quote: Therefore marriage and fornication are not two evils, whereof the second is worse: but marriage and continence are two goods, whereof the second is better
opinions.translation: C.L. Cornish, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits sharply: Catholics and Orthodox keep a high place for vowed celibacy; most Protestants and most non-religious people reject ranking singleness above marriage.

opinions.position: Refuse even justified anger. Anger nursed against someone turns into hatred without your noticing, because no angry person thinks his anger unjust.
opinions.side_note: Strict side: do not trust 'righteous' anger in yourself.
opinions.quote: Wherefore it is much better for us to forbear from anger, even when one has given us just occasion for it, than, beginning with what seems just anger against any one, to fall, through this occult tendency of passion, into hating him.
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits people: many today think anger at injustice is healthy and should be expressed; others, including many Christians and Buddhists, would agree with him.

opinions.position: Christians should feel fear, desire, grief and joy; what matters is that the love behind them is rightly placed. A state of feeling nothing would be worse than every vice.
opinions.side_note: Against the Stoic and monastic ideal of apatheia (passionlessness) as a goal for this life.
opinions.quote: the citizens of the holy city of God, who live according to God in the pilgrimage of this life, both fear and desire, and grieve and rejoice. And because their love is rightly placed, all these affections of theirs are right.
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree emotions are good; the Fathers are split (Evagrius and the desert tradition prize apatheia).

opinions.position: Believe first in order to understand. Understanding is the reward of faith, not its entry ticket. He still spent his life reasoning about faith.
opinions.side_note: Faith-first side, but not anti-reason: 'faith seeking understanding' begins here.
opinions.quote: For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that you may understand
opinions.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
opinions.translation: John Gibb, NPNF1 vol. 7 (1888), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits sharply: many modern people think you should understand before you believe; many believers think some trust has to come first.

opinions.position: Hell is eternal. If eternal life never ends, eternal punishment never ends either, since Christ used the same word for both in one sentence. He calls those who hope all will be saved 'tender-hearted Christians' and treats them gently, but says they are wrong, and rejects Origen's view outright.
opinions.side_note: Against universal salvation (against Origen and Gregory of Nyssa).
opinions.quote: If both destinies are eternal, then we must either understand both as long-continued but at last terminating, or both as endless. For they are correlative — on the one hand, punishment eternal, on the other hand, life eternal. And to say in one and the same sense, life eternal shall be endless, punishment eternal shall come to an end, is the height of absurdity.
opinions.location: Book XXI, chapter 23 (see also chapter 17 on 'those tender-hearted Christians')
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: most traditional churches affirm eternal punishment; a growing number of Christians and most non-religious people reject it.

opinions.position: People before Christ, in any time and place, who believed in Him in whatever way they knew Him and lived justly by His precepts, were saved through Him.
opinions.side_note: A relatively open answer about the past (the holy pagans and patriarchs), though salvation is still only through Christ. Paired with the hard line on unbaptised infants below.
opinions.quote: Therefore, from the beginning of the human race, whosoever believed in Him, and in any way knew Him, and lived in a pious and just manner according to His precepts, was undoubtedly saved by Him, in whatever time and place he may have lived.
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, including most Christians, hope that good people who never heard the gospel can be saved; a minority of Christians say no.

opinions.position: Babies who die unbaptised are not saved; they bear original sin and receive the mildest punishment of all.
opinions.side_note: The hardest-line patristic view on this question; the later Western idea of 'limbo' softened it, and today the Catholic Church speaks of hope for such infants.
opinions.quote: And, of course, the mildest punishment of all will fall upon those who have added no actual sin, to the original sin they brought with them
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone today rejects this, including most churches. One-sided now; useful as a 'sparring' marker, not as a statement most would affirm.

opinions.position: Everything good we do is God's gift; even the first step of faith is given, not earned. We can only pray: give what You command. When Pelagius heard this line quoted in Rome he could not stand it and nearly quarrelled over it.
opinions.side_note: The grace side, against Pelagius. CHANGE OF MIND: he says he once thought the beginning of faith was our own, and changed around 396 while answering Simplicianus: 'I both perceived and asserted that the beginning of faith is God's gift.'
opinions.quote: Give what You command, and command what You will.
opinions.location: Book X, chapter 29 (40); his account of Pelagius's reaction is in On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: many Christians (especially Reformed and Lutheran) agree strongly; many ordinary people and many Christians feel that effort and choice must count for something.

opinions.position: Miracles still happen in Christ's name. He had narratives of healings at the shrine of St Stephen written down and read in church: almost seventy at Hippo in under two years.
opinions.side_note: CHANGE OF MIND: in On True Religion (390) he wrote that the miracles were not allowed to last into our times; in the Retractations he corrected this, and City of God XXII.8 (c. 426) lists many contemporary healings.
opinions.quote: For when I saw, in our own times, frequent signs of the presence of divine powers similar to those which had been given of old, I desired that narratives might be written, judging that the multitude should not remain ignorant of these things.
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: Pentecostals, Catholics and Orthodox expect miracles now; many Protestants (cessationists) and most secular people do not.

opinions.position: His correction of his own earlier claim that miracles had ceased.
opinions.side_note: The later view; the earlier view is quoted inside this passage.
opinions.quote: What I said is not to be taken to mean that no miracles are to be believed to happen now in the name of Christ. For when I wrote that very book, I myself already knew that a blind man had been given his sight at the bodies of the martyrs in Milan.
opinions.original: Sed non sic accipiendum est quod dixi, ut nunc in Christi nomine fieri miracula nulla credantur. Nam ego ipse, quando istum ipsum librum scripsi, ad Mediolanensium corpora martyrum in eadem civitate caecum illuminatum fuisse iam noveram
opinions.location: Book I, chapter 13, section 7 (on On True Religion)
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: As above.

opinions.position: Read Scripture literally unless the literal sense would contradict good morals or true doctrine; then take it as figurative. Love of God and neighbour is the test.
opinions.side_note: A middle rule between strict literalism and free allegory.
opinions.quote: Whatever there is in the word of God that cannot, when taken literally, be referred either to purity of life or soundness of doctrine, you may set down as figurative.
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: literalist Christians would resist it; most mainline Christians and non-believers would accept something like it.

opinions.position: The Church on earth is a mixed body. Good and bad, true and false Christians are tangled together until the last judgment, and no one should split the Church to make it pure.
opinions.side_note: Mixed-church side, against the Donatists (and Novatian's legacy).
opinions.quote: In truth, these two cities are entangled together in this world, and intermixed until the last judgment effects their separation.
opinions.location: Book I, chapter 35; compare Letter 93 on the wheat and tares
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: many Christians prefer strict, committed congregations and leave churches over tolerated sin; others accept a mixed church.

opinions.position: What matters is the root of love, not how an action looks. A father who beats and a kidnapper who caresses can be told apart only by love. So correct, spare, speak or stay silent: but do it from love.
opinions.side_note: Correction-is-love side; he also admits (Letter 95.3) he cannot tell whether punishment improves more people than it harms.
opinions.quote: Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare
opinions.work: Homilies on the First Epistle of John
opinions.translation: H. Browne, NPNF1 vol. 7 (1888), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: The slogan is popular; the context (it justifies firm correction, even blows) would split people, and most today reject physical punishment.

opinions.position: He admits that he does not know whether punishment makes more people better or worse.
opinions.side_note: An honest note of doubt from the same man who defended coercion.
opinions.quote: Besides, I know not whether a greater number have been improved or made worse when alarmed under threats of such punishment at the hands of men as is an object of fear.
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits along the familiar lines of the debate over punishment in parenting and justice.

opinions.position: Clergy may not abandon a flock that still needs them when invaders come. Those who can escape may, but the ministry must not be deserted; the one who runs from the wolf is the hireling.
opinions.side_note: Stay-with-the-flock side (with Cyprian's critics; compare Athanasius's defence of his own flight).
opinions.quote: For I said that those who desire to withdraw to places of safety, if they are able, should not be prevented, and that the ties of our ministry, by which the love of Christ has bound us not to desert the churches which we ought to serve, should not be broken.
opinions.work: Letter 228, to Honoratus (quoted in Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 30)
opinions.translation: Herbert T. Weiskotten (1919)
opinions.today: Most people admire leaders who stay; many would also say a pastor with a family should be free to flee. Splits.

opinions.position: Everything God made is good in its place, even fire, frost, wild beasts and poison. What harms us does so because we misuse it or because of our fallen weakness, not because nature is evil.
opinions.side_note: Against the Manichaean view that parts of nature are evil.
opinions.quote: They do not consider how admirable these things are in their own places, how excellent in their own natures, how beautifully adjusted to the rest of creation, and how much grace they contribute to the universe by their own contributions as to a commonwealth
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree nature is good; the harder question (are suffering and predators part of a good design?) splits believers and unbelievers.

opinions.position: The body is not the cause of sin. The flesh is not evil in itself; it was the sinful soul that made the flesh corruptible, not the flesh that made the soul sinful.
opinions.side_note: Against Platonists and Manichaeans who blamed the body; puts the fault in the will.
opinions.quote: it was not the corruptible flesh that made the soul sinful, but the sinful soul that made the flesh corruptible.
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would agree the body is not evil; many still assume that temptation 'comes from the body'.

opinions.position: Friendship is one of the sweetest goods of life: talking, joking, reading together, disagreeing without ill-humour. But only love for a friend 'in God' cannot be lost.
opinions.side_note: Warm, but with a warning drawn from the grief of losing a friend.
opinions.quote: to discourse and jest with them; to indulge in an interchange of kindnesses; to read together pleasant books; together to trifle, and together to be earnest; to differ at times without ill-humour, as a man would do with his own self
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone agrees friendship is good; the claim that it is safe only when loved 'in God' splits believers from others.

opinions.position: The greatest gift you can give is to forgive from the heart someone who has wronged you, and to wish well and do good to your enemy.
opinions.side_note: Classical Christian position; he calls forgiveness the greatest of all alms.
opinions.quote: But none of those is greater than to forgive from the heart a sin that has been committed against us.
opinions.translation: J.F. Shaw, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree in principle; many today add that forgiveness should not be demanded of victims, so the strength of the claim splits people.

opinions.position: Speaking ill of someone who is not there to answer is not allowed at his table.
opinions.side_note: Recorded practice, carved on his table and enforced (Possidius).
opinions.quote:
Who injures the name of an absent friend
May not at this table as guest attend.
opinions.translation: Herbert T. Weiskotten (1919)
opinions.today: Most agree gossip is bad; few would walk out of dinner over it. The strength of his rule is what divides.

opinions.position: Monks must work with their hands and not live off others. For himself, he says he would far rather do set hours of manual work like a monk than spend his days judging other people's lawsuits.
opinions.side_note: Against monks who refused work in the name of prayer.
opinions.quote: I would much rather every day at certain hours, as much as is appointed by rule in well-governed monasteries, do some work with my hands, and have the remaining hours free for reading and praying, or some work pertaining to Divine Letters, than have to hear these most annoying perplexities of other men's causes about secular matters
opinions.translation: H. Browne, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree everyone should work; whether manual work is better for the soul than office work splits people.

opinions.position: Christians who lost everything when Rome was sacked lost nothing that mattered, if they had held their goods as not holding them. He refused legacies that he thought should go to the dead man's children, and never bought land for the church.
opinions.side_note: Detachment rather than total renunciation for lay people; for himself and his clergy, common life and no private property.
opinions.quote: They, then, who lost their worldly all in the sack of Rome, if they owned their possessions as they had been taught by the apostle, who himself was poor without, but rich within — that is to say, if they used the world as not using it — could say in the words of Job, heavily tried, but not overcome: Naked came I
opinions.location: Book I, chapter 10; practice recorded in Possidius, Life, chapter 24
opinions.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree one should hold possessions loosely; few think the rich must give everything up. Splits more on how much than on whether.

opinions.topic: new: keeping distance from the opposite sex
opinions.position: No woman lived in or stayed at his house, not even his widowed sister, a nun. He said the problem was not his sister but the servants and visitors who would follow, and the talk and temptation they might give the weak.
opinions.side_note: Strict prudence about appearances; compare modern 'Billy Graham rule' debates.
opinions.quote: No woman ever lived or stayed in Augustine's house, not even his own sister, though she was a widow who had long served God and lived in charge of His handmaidens
opinions.translation: Herbert T. Weiskotten (1919)
opinions.today: Splits sharply: some Christians keep such rules for leaders; many people see them as insulting to women or excessive.

sparring.over: Whether Paul's rebuke of Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2) was staged, which Augustine said would put a lie in Scripture; also Jerome's new translation from the Hebrew, which nearly caused a riot at Oea when a bishop read 'ivy' for Jonah's 'gourd'. Jerome told him to stop 'annoying an old man'.
sparring.source: Augustine, Letters 28, 40, 71, 82; Jerome, Letters 72, 75 (in Augustine's collection)

sparring.over: Grace and free will. Pelagius could not bear Augustine's prayer 'Give what You command, and command what You will' and nearly quarrelled with a bishop who quoted it; Augustine wrote against him for the rest of his life.
sparring.source: On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53; On Nature and Grace

sparring.over: Original sin, sex and infant damnation; a bitter decade-long exchange of books that was still unfinished when Augustine died (the Unfinished Work against Julian).
sparring.source: Against Julian; Unfinished Work against Julian

sparring.over: Whether the Church must be pure, whether sacraments by unworthy clergy are valid, and whether the state may pressure schismatics. Vincentius was an old acquaintance from his student days.
sparring.source: Letter 93 to Vincentius; Possidius, Life, chapters 9-14

sparring.with: Faustus and Fortunatus (Manichaeans; Augustine himself had been a Manichaean for nine years)
sparring.over: Whether the Old Testament God is good, whether matter is evil, and war in the Old Testament. He wrote thirty-three books against Faustus and debated Fortunatus in public at Hippo.
sparring.source: Reply to Faustus; Possidius, Life, chapter 6

sparring.over: Whether being buried near a martyr helps the dead. Augustine answered that such care comforts the living but the dead are helped by prayers and alms, not location.
sparring.source: On the Care to be Had for the Dead, section 1 onward

portraits.title: Fresco of Augustine, the oldest known portrait of him
Saint Augustine in His Study (Ognissanti, Florence)

figures.name: Boethius
also_known_as: St Severinus Boethius (in the diocese of Pavia)
figures.places: Rome (senatorial family, raised in the house of Symmachus); Ravenna (the Gothic court of Theodoric); imprisoned at Pavia and executed in the ager Calventianus nearby; buried in San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro, Pavia
figures.role: Roman senator, consul (510) and Master of Offices under the Arian Gothic king Theodoric; philosopher, translator of Aristotle's logic, author of the theological tractates and the Consolation of Philosophy
figures.status_note: Venerated as a martyr, St Severinus Boethius, in the diocese of Pavia (feast 23 October); the cult was confirmed by Rome in 1883. He is not in the general Roman calendar and has no cult in the Orthodox Church. Cautions for a reader: he was executed on a charge of treason (supporting the senate against the king), not for the faith as such, so calling him a martyr is a local tradition. The Consolation argues from philosophy alone and never names Christ; most of its teaching is spoken by Lady Philosophy, who corrects the complaining prisoner 'Boethius', so the prisoner's complaints are the view being corrected and Philosophy's answers are the book's settled view. Some of her teaching is Platonist (hints of the soul's recollection of prior knowledge, and the phrase that the happy are 'gods' by participation). His five theological tractates, whose authenticity is now generally accepted, show him an orthodox Catholic Christian.
figures.hook: The most powerful civil servant in Gothic Italy was condemned without a hearing, and in his cell awaiting a brutal death he wrote a book in which Philosophy walks in and throws out the Muses of self-pity.

stories.story: In 522 his two young sons were made joint consuls, a rare honour. He gave the speech praising the king in the senate and sat between the two consuls at the Circus. Within about a year he was a prisoner. Lady Philosophy reminds him of that day in the Consolation.
stories.source: Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 3

stories.story: When the informer Cyprian accused the senator Albinus of treasonable letters to the Emperor Justin, Boethius spoke up before the king: 'Cyprian's charge is false. But if Albinus did it, then I and the whole senate did it with one mind. It is false, lord king.' Cyprian then produced false witnesses against Boethius too, and the king believed them over the senators.
stories.source: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, sections 85-86 (chapter 14 on The Latin Library); own rendering

stories.story: He was sentenced without being heard. The same chronicle says a cord was tightened round his forehead until his eyes started from his head, and then he was killed with a club.
stories.source: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, section 87; also the epilogue to H.R. James's translation (1897)

stories.story: King Theodoric asked him to build a water-clock and a sundial as a diplomatic gift for Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, and to choose a first-rate harper for Clovis, king of the Franks. Theodoric's letter praises him for putting Pythagoras, Ptolemy, Euclid, Plato, Aristotle and Archimedes into Latin.
stories.source: Cassiodorus, Variae I.45 and II.40 (tr. Thomas Hodgkin, 1886)

stories.story: At a church assembly in Rome a letter from Eastern bishops was read about Christ's two natures. Everyone loudly insisted the answer was obvious. Boethius, who could not see the face of the man whose opinion he wanted, kept silent rather than pretend to know, went home, and chewed on the question until he solved it: the result is his treatise against Eutyches and Nestorius.
stories.source: Against Eutyches and Nestorius, preface (tr. Stewart and Rand, 1918)

stories.story: As a high official he blocked the king's steward Triggvilla and the official Conigastus from preying on the weak, and when a forced grain sale threatened Campania with famine he fought the praetorian prefect before the king and won. He believed these fights made the enemies who later destroyed him.
stories.source: Consolation of Philosophy, Book I, prose 4

stories.story: The Consolation opens with the prisoner in tears, the Muses of poetry at his bedside dictating laments. A tall woman appears, Philosophy, sees them, and in anger drives them out as 'play-acting wantons' who feed his sickness with sweet poison, and then begins to cure him with reason.
stories.source: Consolation of Philosophy, Book I, prose 1

temperament.trait: Proud, aloof intellectual who wrote for the few
temperament.evidence: He tells his father-in-law Symmachus he wraps his theology in 'new and unaccustomed words which speak only to you and to myself... The rest of the world I simply disregard: they cannot understand, and therefore do not deserve to read.'
temperament.source: On the Trinity, preface (tr. Stewart and Rand, 1918)

temperament.trait: Principled public man who did not mind offending the powerful
temperament.evidence: 'I have had to think nothing of giving offence to the powerful in the cause of justice. How often have I encountered and balked Conigastus in his assaults on the fortunes of the weak?'

He tied his own fate to the accused Albinus and the senate in front of the king; in the Consolation he says he would have answered like Canius: had he known of a plot, the tyrant would never have known.

temperament.trait: Could sink into self-pity, and wrote a book about climbing out of it
temperament.evidence: The prisoner begins by writing laments with the Muses and complains bitterly; Philosophy's first act is to stop the self-pity. He admits: 'in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy.'
temperament.source: Consolation, Book I, prose 1; Book II, prose 4

temperament.trait: Quiet in a crowd; would rather keep silent than bluff
temperament.evidence: At the assembly: 'being overwhelmed by the mob of ignorant speakers, I held my peace, fearing lest I should be rightly set down as insane if I held out for being sane among those madmen.'
Asked by the king to build a water-clock and sundial for a foreign king; wrote textbooks on arithmetic and music and translated Greek logic, aiming to put all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin.
temperament.source: Cassiodorus, Variae I.45; Stewart and Rand, introduction (1918)

genuine_lines.quote: For truly in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy.
genuine_lines.location: Book II, prose 4 (spoken by the prisoner)
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897); James echoes Hamlet here, the Latin is 'nihil est miserum nisi cum putes'

genuine_lines.quote: For truly I believe that Ill Fortune is of more use to men than Good Fortune.
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: Cease, then, to seek the wealth thou hast lost, since in true friends thou hast found the most precious of all riches.
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: Wouldst thou give each his due; then know Thy love the good must have, the bad thy pity claim.
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge who seeth all things.
genuine_lines.location: Book V, prose 6 (the last words of the book)
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: The other, with biting sarcasm, retorted: "I should have hadst thou held thy peace."
genuine_lines.location: Book II, prose 7 (the anecdote behind 'if you had kept silent you would have stayed a philosopher')
genuine_lines.translation: H.R. James (1897)

genuine_lines.quote: But if you are in any point of another opinion, examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.
genuine_lines.work: Whether Father, Son and Holy Spirit are Substantially Predicated of the Godhead (Tractate II)
genuine_lines.translation: H.F. Stewart and E.K. Rand, Loeb (1918)

misattributed.line: There is no greater sorrow than to remember happy times in misery (usually credited to Dante).
misattributed.truth: Dante's Francesca says it (Inferno V.121-123), but Dante took it from Boethius: 'in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy' (Consolation II prose 4). The misattribution runs the other way: people credit Dante with Boethius's thought.

misattributed.line: If you had kept silent, you would have remained a philosopher (Si tacuisses, philosophus mansisses).
misattributed.truth: Not a sentence Boethius wrote as his own maxim. The Latin proverb grew out of an anecdote he tells in Consolation II prose 7 about a man who called himself a philosopher; the punchline there is 'I should have [known it] hadst thou held thy peace.'

misattributed.line: On the Discipline of Scholars (De disciplina scholarium), once printed under Boethius's name.
misattributed.truth: A 13th-century work, not by Boethius; it was widely read in medieval universities as his.

misattributed.line: Boethius died a martyr for the Christian faith at the hands of an Arian heretic king.
misattributed.truth: An overstatement. The sources say he was condemned on a treason charge after defending a senator accused of plotting with Constantinople. Theodoric was an Arian, and later tradition read the death as martyrdom, which Pavia still honours, but no contemporary source says he died for his faith.

opinions.position: Good and wise people have a duty to enter public life, or government falls to the worst. He took office to put philosophy into practice, protect the weak and resist corruption, and he paid for it.
opinions.side_note: Pro-public-service side (against flight from office). The line is Philosophy's teaching which he says he followed.
opinions.quote: By his mouth likewise thou didst point out this imperative reason why philosophers should enter public life, to wit, lest, if the reins of government be left to unprincipled and profligate citizens, trouble and destruction should come upon the good.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people agree good people should serve; many Christians today are wary of politics as corrupting. Splits.

opinions.position: Money is worth something only when it is given away, and once given it is no longer yours. Riches cannot satisfy: 'He is never rich whose fear / Sees grim Want forever near.'
opinions.side_note: Detachment side, argued from philosophy.
opinions.quote: then money is only precious when it is given away, and, by being transferred to others, ceases to be one's own.
opinions.location: Book II, prose 5 (Philosophy); compare Book II, metre 2
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people agree money does not bring happiness; most also want it. The claim that wealth has no value until given away is a minority view.

opinions.position: Bad fortune does more good than good fortune. Good fortune always lies; bad fortune tells the truth, teaches, and shows you who your real friends are.
opinions.side_note: A strong claim; the Fathers broadly agree that trials help, but few say it this starkly.
opinions.quote: For truly I believe that Ill Fortune is of more use to men than Good Fortune. For Good Fortune, when she wears the guise of happiness, and most seems to caress, is always lying; Ill Fortune is always truthful, since, in changing, she shows her inconstancy. The one deceives, the other teaches
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Splits well: many people say hardship made them who they are; many others think suffering mostly harms and should not be praised.

opinions.position: Fame is worthless. The whole earth is a dot compared with the heavens, and only a tiny part of it is inhabited, so seeking renown is seeking glory in a pin-prick.
opinions.side_note: Contempt for reputation (a Stoic and Christian theme).
opinions.quote: You, then, who are shut in and prisoned in this merest fraction of a point's space, do ye take thought for the blazoning of your fame, for the spreading abroad of your renown?
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Splits: many people want to be known or to leave a legacy; others find the pursuit of fame empty.

opinions.position: Bodily pleasures cannot make anyone happy. Craving them is restless, getting them brings regret, and if pleasure were happiness then animals would be the happiest of all.
opinions.side_note: Against pleasure as the good (a stricter view than Augustine's use-and-enjoy).
opinions.quote: what shall I say of the pleasures of the body? The lust thereof is full of uneasiness; the sating, of repentance.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people today would say pleasure is part of a good life, though not all of it; the view that bodily pleasure mostly ends in regret is a minority one.

opinions.position: Even the sweetness of wife and children cannot guarantee happiness; some find their tormentors in their sons, and Euripides was right that the childless are lucky in their misfortune.
opinions.side_note: A startlingly cool line for a devoted father of two consuls; spoken by Philosophy to show no earthly good is secure.
opinions.quote: I know, indeed, that the sweetness of wife and children should be right comely, yet only too true to nature is what was said of one—that he found in his sons his tormentors.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Splits: most parents would reject it; research on parenting and happiness is genuinely mixed, and some people today choose to be childless for similar reasons.

opinions.position: No wise person hates anyone. Wickedness is a sickness of the soul, so the wicked deserve pity, as the physically sick do, not hatred.
opinions.side_note: Pity-not-hatred side.
opinions.quote: Whence it comes to pass that for the wise no place is left for hatred; only the most foolish would hate the good, and to hate the bad is unreasonable.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Many people agree hatred is wrong; many also think some anger at evildoers is right. Splits.

opinions.position: Most wars are senseless. Men attack each other with no right or reason except that their lands and laws differ, though death comes soon enough anyway.
opinions.side_note: Closer to the anti-war side than Augustine; he does not discuss just war.
opinions.quote: Unjust and cruel wars they wage, And haste with flying darts the death to meet or deal. No right nor reason can they show; 'Tis but because their lands and laws are not the same.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people today agree many wars are unjust; they split on whether any war is justified.

opinions.position: Punishment is good for the wicked. Wrongdoers who escape punishment are more wretched than those who are justly punished; if they could see clearly they would hand themselves over to their judges.
opinions.side_note: Punishment-as-medicine side (from Plato's Gorgias).
opinions.quote: Then, the wicked are far more unhappy when indulged with an unjust freedom from punishment than when punished by a just retribution.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Splits well: many people think punishment is only for deterrence or protection; others agree that being held to account is good for the guilty person.

opinions.position: Faith and reason should be joined. He argued theology with the tools of logic and asked readers to reconcile faith and reason if they could; in prison he let himself ask God the hardest question: why do evil men triumph over the innocent while God watches?
opinions.side_note: Reason-friendly side; the prisoner's complaint about evil is a question Philosophy then answers, not a denial.
opinions.quote: But if you are in any point of another opinion, examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.
opinions.work: Tractate II (Whether Father, Son and Holy Spirit are Substantially Predicated of the Godhead)
opinions.location: closing words; compare Consolation I prose 4: 'If God exists, whence comes evil? Yet whence comes good, if He exists not?'
opinions.translation: H.F. Stewart and E.K. Rand, Loeb (1918)
opinions.today: Most educated people today favour reason; some believers distrust applying logic to faith. Splits.

opinions.position: We have free will. A creature that can reason must be able to choose, and God's foreknowledge does not force our choices, because God sees all time at once as an eternal present.
opinions.side_note: Free-will side; his solution (eternity as a single present) became the classic Christian answer.
opinions.quote: nor, indeed, can any creature be rational, unless he be endowed with free will.
opinions.location: Book V, prose 2 (Philosophy); the eternity argument is V prose 6
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people believe in free will; some Christians (strong predestinarians) and many scientists and philosophers (determinists) do not.

opinions.position: Prayer and hope are not wasted, even though God foreknows everything. Rightly directed, they cannot fail.
opinions.side_note: Pro-petitionary-prayer side, against the fatalism that foreknowledge seems to imply.
opinions.quote: Our hopes and prayers also are not fixed on God in vain, and when they are rightly directed cannot fail of effect.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Believers mostly agree; many people doubt prayer changes anything. Splits by belief.

opinions.position: Indulging grief in poetry and lament feeds the sickness it seems to soothe. The cure for sorrow is reason, not the Muses.
opinions.side_note: Stoic-leaning side, against 'having a good cry' through art; contrast Augustine's defence of tears.
opinions.quote: has allowed yon play-acting wantons to approach this sick man—these who, so far from giving medicine to heal his malady, even feed it with sweet poison? These it is who kill the rich crop of reason with the barren thorns of passion
opinions.location: Book I, prose 1 (Philosophy, of the Muses of poetry)
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Most people today think expressing sorrow in words, music or art helps healing; the opposite view is a minority. Good sparring marker.

opinions.topic: new: explain the faith to everyone, or only to the few
opinions.position: Deep matters should be written for the few who can understand them. He deliberately used compressed, technical language so that only his father-in-law could follow, and said the rest did not deserve to read.
opinions.side_note: Elitist side; contrast Augustine's and Chrysostom's preaching to ordinary crowds.
opinions.quote: So I purposely use brevity and wrap up the ideas I draw from the deep questionings of philosophy in new and unaccustomed words which speak only to you and to myself, that is, if you deign to look at them. The rest of the world I simply disregard: they cannot understand, and therefore do not deserve to read.
opinions.translation: H.F. Stewart and E.K. Rand, Loeb (1918)
opinions.today: Most people today dislike this; some academics and specialists quietly agree. Strong sparring marker.

opinions.topic: new: happiness is in how you take it
opinions.position: Nothing is miserable unless you think it so, and any lot is happy if borne calmly. The place you call exile is home to the people who live there.
opinions.side_note: Stoic side of the question 'do circumstances or attitudes make us happy?'
opinions.quote: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Splits well: popular psychology and CBT lean his way; many people feel it dismisses real suffering and injustice.

opinions.position: True friends are the most precious wealth, and misfortune is useful because it shows who they are.
opinions.side_note: Shared with Augustine and Paulinus.
opinions.quote: Cease, then, to seek the wealth thou hast lost, since in true friends thou hast found the most precious of all riches.
opinions.translation: H.R. James (1897)
opinions.today: Almost universally agreed; tells the quiz little on its own.

opinions.position: Stand with the accused rather than save yourself. Before the king he declared that if Albinus was guilty, he and the whole senate were guilty too; in the Consolation he says that had he known of a plot, he would never have informed.
opinions.side_note: Loyalty-and-candour side. Not a claim about lying: the Canius line is a refusal to inform.
opinions.quote: Cyprian's charge is false. But if Albinus did it, then I and the whole senate did it with one mind. It is false, lord king.
opinions.original: Falsa est insinuatio Cypriani; sed si Albinus fecit, et ego et cunctus senatus uno consilio fecimus; falsum est, domne rex.
opinions.work: Anonymus Valesianus (a near-contemporary chronicle of Theodoric's reign)
opinions.location: part 2, section 85 (chapter 14 on The Latin Library); compare Consolation I prose 4 (Canius: 'If I had known,' said he, 'thou shouldst never have known')
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Most people admire it; many would also say it is foolish to sink with someone else. Splits on prudence versus loyalty.

opinions.position: Better to keep quiet than join a loud crowd that pretends to know. He held his peace in the assembly, then worked the problem out in private.
opinions.side_note: Silence as intellectual honesty rather than as monastic practice.
opinions.quote: I was, I admit, much put out, and being overwhelmed by the mob of ignorant speakers, I held my peace, fearing lest I should be rightly set down as insane if I held out for being sane among those madmen.
opinions.translation: H.F. Stewart and E.K. Rand, Loeb (1918)
opinions.today: Splits: some people speak up whatever the room thinks; others keep quiet until they are sure.

sparring.with: Eutyches and Nestorius (in writing; both long dead)
sparring.over: How Christ is both God and man. He wrote a treatise refuting both extremes after an assembly in Rome where no one could explain the difference between 'from two natures' and 'in two natures'.
sparring.source: Against Eutyches and Nestorius, preface and body

sparring.with: Cyprian the referendarius (and the informers Basilius, Opilio and Gaudentius)
sparring.over: The treason charge against Albinus and the senate. Cyprian produced false witnesses against Boethius; the Consolation names the informers with contempt.

sparring.with: Conigastus and Triggvilla (officials at Theodoric's court)
sparring.over: Their oppression of the weak and their schemes, which Boethius says he repeatedly blocked.
Loyalty to the Roman senate versus the Gothic crown; Theodoric condemned him without a hearing.

portraits.title: Philosophy Presenting the Seven Liberal Arts to Boethius (J. Paul Getty Museum)
Boethius teaching his students (initial in an Italian Consolation manuscript, Glasgow University Library MS Hunter 374)
Wheel of Fortune; Boethius on his sickbed (Utrecht University Library Hs. 1335)

figures.name: Paulinus of Nola
figures.places: Born near Bordeaux (Aquitaine); senator at Rome and governor of Campania (c. 381); lived in Spain (his infant son buried at Complutum; ordained at Barcelona, Christmas 394); settled at the tomb of St Felix at Nola (Cimitile, near Naples) from 395; bishop of Nola from about 409
figures.role: Senator and poet, pupil of the poet Ausonius, who gave away a great fortune with his wife Therasia; lived as a monk at a saint's shrine, then became its bishop; letter-writer to Augustine, Jerome, Sulpicius Severus and many others; the first great Christian Latin lyric poet of the saints
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches (22 June). No condemnation. Cautions for a reader: he was a friend of people later judged heretical: he loved Pelagius as a servant of God until Augustine and Alypius wrote to warn him (Letter 186, 417), and he wrote the wedding poem for Julian of Eclanum, who became Pelagius's fiercest defender. Only a few of his words survive in pre-1929 English (his letters to Augustine in NPNF; lines reported by Augustine; Ambrose and Gregory tell stories about him); most of his letters and poems exist in English only in modern copyrighted translations (Walsh, 1966-75), so most quotations below are my own renderings from Hartel's Latin (CSEL 29-30, 1894). The famous story that he sold himself as a slave to the Vandals to free a widow's son (Gregory, Dialogues III.1) cannot be true of him as told: the Vandals raided Campania in 455, after his death.
figures.hook: A Roman senator gave away one of the great fortunes of the West, spent thirty-five years at a country saint's tomb writing him a birthday poem every year, and when the Goths took him prisoner his only prayer was not to be tortured for gold, 'for where all my treasure is You know.'

stories.story: He and his wife Therasia sold their estates and gave the money to the poor. Ambrose of Milan wrote that Paulinus 'has sold both his own possessions and those of his wife' and asked what the great men of the world would say: that a man of such family and eloquence should leave the senate and let a noble line die out was 'not to be borne'.
stories.source: Ambrose, Letter 58, to Sabinus (Oxford Library of the Fathers, 1881)

stories.story: On Christmas Day 394 the crowd in the church at Barcelona suddenly seized him and had him ordained priest. He says he was unwilling, not from pride: he had wanted to begin as a church doorkeeper. He agreed on condition that he would not be tied to Barcelona.
stories.source: Paulinus, Letter 1 to Sulpicius Severus, section 10 (CSEL 29); own rendering

stories.story: His old teacher, the poet Ausonius, wrote letter after hurt letter begging him to come back to poetry, friends and public life, and hinted that his wife had led him astray. Paulinus answered in verse: hearts vowed to Christ are closed to Apollo; my wife is no Tanaquil but a Lucretia; if this pleases you, rejoice, and if not, leave me to Christ. He also promised to hold Ausonius in his heart for as long as he lived and beyond.
stories.source: Paulinus, Carmina 10 and 11

stories.story: When the Goths sacked Nola in 410 and took him prisoner, he prayed silently, as he later told Augustine: 'O Lord, let me not be troubled for gold and silver, for where all my treasure is You know.' Augustine used the story in the City of God.
stories.source: Augustine, City of God, Book I, chapter 10

stories.story: He and Therasia had a longed-for son, Celsus, who died eight days old in Spain. They buried him at Complutum beside the martyrs there. Years later, consoling other parents whose boy Celsus died at eight, he wrote that their son had lived as many years as his own had lived days.
stories.source: Paulinus, Carmen 31, lines 601-620 (CSEL 30)

stories.story: He wrote a birthday poem (a natalicium) for St Felix every 14 January, marking the saint's heavenly birthday. In them he describes crowds pouring into Nola from Lucania, Apulia, Calabria and all of Campania, walking through the night with torches.
stories.source: Paulinus, Carmen 14 (Natalicium 3) and the other natalicia

stories.story: Country people came to Felix's feast and drank all night at the tombs. Rather than ban them, he had Bible stories painted round the new church with captions, so the crowds would spend the hours looking and reading and drink less.
stories.source: Paulinus, Carmen 27, lines 542-595 (CSEL 30)

stories.story: He sent Augustine, whom he had never met, a loaf of bread as a sign of their oneness of heart, with his first letter praising Augustine's books against the Manichaeans. They corresponded for over twenty years and never met.
stories.source: Paulinus, Letter to Augustine (Augustine, Letter 25.5)

stories.story: A later legend: when the Vandals carried off the son of a poor widow, Paulinus, having given away everything, went to Africa and offered himself as a slave in the boy's place. He worked as a gardener until the king recognised him and freed him with all the captives of Nola. The story is told as he heard it from 'holy elders'; it is chronologically impossible for this Paulinus.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book III, chapter 1 (1608 translation, revised 1911)

stories.story: At his death in 431, the priest Uranius reports, he said the psalm verse 'I have prepared a lamp for my Christ' at the hour the evening lamps were lit, and died towards midnight.
stories.source: Uranius, On the Death of Paulinus (De obitu Paulini), to Pacatus, 432 (Latin in Migne PL 53); secondary report only

temperament.trait: Warm and effusive in friendship, even with people he never met
temperament.evidence: He tells Augustine, whom he knew only through books, that they are near though distant and known though unknown, and sends him bread; Augustine replied that everyone who read Paulinus's letter 'carry it away with them, because, while they read, it carries them away.'
He signs his letters with his wife: 'To Augustine, Our Lord and Brother Beloved and Venerable, from Paulinus and Therasia, Sinners.' He calls himself 'this infant creeping on the ground'.
temperament.source: Augustine, Letter 25 (from Paulinus), heading and section 3

temperament.evidence: Taken prisoner in the sack of Nola, his only prayer was not to be tormented for gold, since his treasure was with God.

temperament.trait: Gentle and indulgent with simple people
temperament.evidence: Faced with peasants drinking at the saints' tombs, he says such joys 'should be forgiven' the unlettered, and tries pictures instead of prohibitions.

temperament.trait: Devoted, even sentimental, to his patron saint
temperament.evidence: Fourteen birthday poems for St Felix survive; he calls Felix his father, lord and patron and builds and decorates his shrine.

temperament.trait: Firm but loving when he disappoints people he loves
temperament.evidence: He refused every plea of his old teacher Ausonius to return, but swore to carry him in his heart even after death.

genuine_lines.quote: O Lord, let me not be troubled for gold and silver, for where all my treasure is You know.
genuine_lines.work: Prayer in captivity, reported by Augustine in City of God ('as he afterwards told me')
genuine_lines.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF1 vol. 2 (1887), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Nor is it strange that though distant we are near, though unknown we are well known to each other; for we are members of one body, having one Head
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I may swim, unhindered by any clothing for the flesh or care for the morrow, across the sea of this present life
genuine_lines.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Why, father, do you bid the Muses I have disowned come back into my care? Hearts vowed to Christ say no to the Camenae and are shut to Apollo.
genuine_lines.original: Quid abdicatas in meam curam, pater, / Redire Musas praecipis? / Negant Camoenis, nec patent Apollini / Dicata Christo pectora.
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Latin

genuine_lines.quote: If this pleases you, rejoice in your friend's rich hope. If not, leave me to be approved by Christ alone.
genuine_lines.original: Si placet hoc, gratare tui spe divite amici: / Si contra est, Christo tantum me linque probari.
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Latin

genuine_lines.quote: So you gathered into the apostle's hall a crowd of the poor who beg for coins all over Rome: the patrons of our souls.
genuine_lines.original: itaque patronos animarum nostrarum pauperes, qui tota Roma stipem meritant, multitudinem in aula apostoli congregasti.
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 29, 1894)

misattributed.line: Paulinus of Nola invented the church bell (hence Latin 'campana', from Campania).
misattributed.truth: No text by Paulinus or anyone of his time mentions bells. The attribution is a much later legend, apparently built on the word 'campana'; Nola's bell-shaped festival towers (the Gigli) keep it alive.

misattributed.line: Paulinus sold himself as a slave to the Vandals to ransom a widow's son.
misattributed.truth: Told by Gregory the Great (Dialogues III.1) on the word of 'holy elders', about 160 years later. The Vandals did not raid Campania until 455, after Paulinus died in 431, so it cannot be true of him as told; some suggest it was borrowed from a later bishop of Nola.

opinions.position: Give it all away. He stripped himself of his fortune so he could 'swim' through life unencumbered, and in captivity his treasure was with God.
opinions.side_note: Total-renunciation side (with Antony and Melania), though see the next entry: he did not condemn the rich who use wealth well.
opinions.quote: I have therefore been at pains to rid myself of all baggage and garments which might impede my progress, in order that, obedient to the command and sustained by the help of Christ, I may swim, unhindered by any clothing for the flesh or care for the morrow, across the sea of this present life
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one today thinks ordinary Christians should give away everything; many admire those who do. A strong sparring marker.

opinions.position: Riches are not the problem; people are blamed or accepted by God according to how they use them. He praised the senator Pammachius for staying rich and using it for the poor.
opinions.side_note: Nuance: renunciation for himself, good use for others.
opinions.quote: Finally, so you may know that it is not riches but people, by the use they make of them, who are blameworthy or acceptable to God, read of the holy fathers
opinions.original: Denique, ut scias non diuitias sed homines pro earum usibus esse culpabiles uel acceptos deo, lege sanctos patres
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 29, 1894)
opinions.today: Most people today agree it is the use of money that matters. Mostly one-sided.

opinions.topic: new: the poor are our patrons
opinions.position: The poor are the patrons of our souls: feeding them is not charity from above but seeking their help. He praised Pammachius for filling St Peter's in Rome with the city's beggars for a funeral feast, and wrote that by nature every human being is neighbour to every other.
opinions.side_note: A reversal of the Roman patron-client system: the rich become the clients of the poor.
opinions.quote: So you gathered into the apostle's hall a crowd of the poor who beg for coins all over Rome: the patrons of our souls.
opinions.original: itaque patronos animarum nostrarum pauperes, qui tota Roma stipem meritant, multitudinem in aula apostoli congregasti.
opinions.location: section 11; compare section 17: 'omnis natura homini homo proximus'
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 29, 1894)
opinions.today: The idea that the giver gains more than the receiver is widely liked; the claim that the poor are spiritually above us divides people.

opinions.position: He turned his back on the classical literature and philosophy he had loved, calling it unprofitable, and refused his teacher's pleas to return to pagan poetry. He kept writing poetry, but only about Christ and the saints.
opinions.side_note: Renouncing side on pagan letters (for himself), close to Jerome's dream; but see the next entry.
opinions.quote: The wisdom of this world I have unhappily hitherto regarded with admiration, and, devoting myself to literature which I now see to be unprofitable, and wisdom which I now reject, I was in the sight of God foolish and dumb.
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would not give up secular literature for faith; a minority of Christians limit their reading to Christian works.

opinions.position: To a cultured friend who read Plato and Cicero but had no time for Christ: you need not throw away philosophy, only season it with faith and become God's philosopher.
opinions.side_note: The more moderate Paulinus (c. 399): learning is not the enemy; misplaced priorities are.
opinions.quote: You have time to be a philosopher but no time to be a Christian. Turn your thinking and your eloquence around instead. You need not lay aside the philosophy of your mind, so long as you season it with faith and religion.
opinions.original: uacat tibi ut et philosophus sis, non uacat ut Christianus sis. uerte potius sententiam, uerte facundiam. nam animi philosophiam non deponas licet, dum eam fide condias et religione
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 29, 1894)
opinions.today: Many people recognise the charge of having time for everything except God; the principle is widely accepted among believers.

opinions.position: He did not seek ordination and was made priest by the sudden force of a crowd, unwillingly, but accepted it as God's doing. He had wanted only the lowest church job, doorkeeper.
opinions.side_note: Reluctant-acceptance side, like Augustine and Ambrose.
