opinions.quote: On the Lord's day on which He deigned to be born in the flesh, I was seized by the sudden force of the crowd (He Himself is my witness), though I believe it was by His ordaining, and made a priest. I confess I was unwilling. It was not that I scorned the place: I call Him to witness that I had wished to begin holy service with the name and duty of a doorkeeper.
opinions.original: post illas litteras quibus rescripsisti die domini, quo nasci carne dignatus est, repentina, ut ipse testis est, ui multitudinis, sed credo ipsius ordinatione correptus et presbyteratu initiatus sum, fateor, inuitus, non fastidio loci (nam tester ipsum, quia et ab aeditui nomine et officio optaui sacram incipere seruitutem)
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 29, 1894)
opinions.today: People today would find forced ordination wrong; the attitude (take the lowest place, accept a call you did not seek) is widely admired.

opinions.position: Follow Christ even when it breaks the heart of the people who formed you. He refused his beloved teacher's pleas to come home to his old life, and answered: be glad for me if you can; if not, Christ's approval is enough.
opinions.side_note: Christ-over-family side, but without breaking the friendship (see his promise in Carmen 11).
opinions.quote: If this pleases you, rejoice in your friend's rich hope. If not, leave me to be approved by Christ alone.
opinions.original: Si placet hoc, gratare tui spe divite amici: / Si contra est, Christo tantum me linque probari.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Splits: many admire following your calling against family wishes; many others think family obligations should come first.

opinions.topic: new: friendship beyond distance and death
opinions.position: True friendship survives distance, disagreement and even death. He promised the teacher whose wishes he refused to carry him in his heart for life and after it.
opinions.side_note: Shared with Augustine's 'friend in God', but warmer and more personal.
opinions.quote: Through all the age that is given and appointed to mortals, as long as I am held in this enclosing body, however wide the world between us, I will keep you planted in my very heart, not far from my sight. I will see you with my heart and embrace you with a loving mind, present to me everywhere. And when I am freed from the prison of the body, in whatever part of the sky our common Father sets me, there too I will carry you in my soul.
opinions.original: Ego te per omne, quod datum mortalibus / Et destinatum seculum est, / Claudente donec continebor corpore, / Discernar orbe quolibet, / Nec orbe longe, nec remotum lumine, / Tenebo fibris insitum, / Videbo corde, mente complectar pia / Ubique praesentem mihi. / Et cum solutus corporali carcere, / Terraque provolavero, / Quo me locarit axe communis Pater, / Illic quoque te animo geram.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Most people hope friendships last; whether you can stay close to someone after refusing their deepest wish splits people.

opinions.position: Care for where the dead are buried is not an empty gesture. He believed burial beside a martyr (he had a young man buried by St Felix for his mother) could help the dead, since the whole Church prays for the departed.
opinions.side_note: The popular pro-shrine view; Augustine, asked to rule on it, answered that it comforts the living and helps the dead only by moving people to pray.
opinions.quote: For you say that to your thinking these be no empty motions of religious and faithful minds, which take this care for their deceased friends. You add, moreover, that it cannot be void of effect that the whole Church is wont to supplicate for the departed
opinions.work: Paulinus's letter, as summarised by Augustine in On the Care to be Had for the Dead
opinions.translation: H. Browne, NPNF1 vol. 3 (1887), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits: Catholics and Orthodox pray for the dead and value burial places; most Protestants and secular people think it makes no difference to the dead.

opinions.position: Paint Bible stories on church walls, with captions, so that unlettered people can learn from them and be drawn from drinking to reading and prayer.
opinions.side_note: Pro-image side, one of the earliest explicit defences of church art as teaching (compare Gregory the Great's 'books of the unlettered'; against Epiphanius, who tore down a painted curtain).
opinions.quote: So we thought it a useful work to brighten all the buildings of Felix with holy pictures, in case the painted forms in colour might catch the amazed minds of the country people, with captions written above, so that the letters show what the hand has set out.
opinions.original: propterea uisum nobis opus utile totis / Felicis domibus pictura ludere sancta, / si forte adtonitas haec per spectacula mentes / agrestum caperet fucata coloribus umbra, / quae super exprimitur titulis, ut littera monstret / quod manus explicuit
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894; OCR slips corrected)
opinions.today: Splits: Catholics and Orthodox love religious art; some Protestants keep churches bare; most people today enjoy art in churches as culture.

opinions.position: Be gentle with the faults of simple people. The country folk drinking at the saints' tombs are wrong, but their error comes from ignorance and devotion, so it should be forgiven and gently redirected rather than punished.
opinions.side_note: Indulgent side. Contrast Ambrose, who banned such tomb-feasts outright (Augustine, Confessions VI.2), and Augustine, who campaigned against them in Africa.
opinions.quote: Still, I think such joys as the little people draw out over their feasts should be forgiven, because error has crept into untaught minds. Their simplicity does not know how great the fault is. It stumbles out of devotion, wrongly believing that the saints are glad when their tombs are drenched in fragrant wine.
opinions.original: ignoscenda tamen puto talia paruis / gaudia quae ducunt epulis, quia mentibus error / inrepsit rudibus; nec tantae conscia culpae / simplicitas pietate cadit, male credula sanctos / perfusis halante mero gaudere sepulchris.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894; OCR slips corrected)
opinions.today: Splits well: some people want clear rules firmly enforced; others would tolerate folk customs and redirect them gently.

opinions.position: A Christian wedding should banish pagan revelry and the old gods of love; marriage is a harmony of souls in chaste love and a peace in tune with God. He and his wife later lived together as brother and sister.
opinions.side_note: Written for the wedding of Julian (later bishop of Eclanum and Pelagian leader) and Titia; the poem also praises virginity.
opinions.quote: Two souls in harmony are joined in chaste love, a boy who is Christ's virgin and a girl who is God's virgin... Far from this bridal room be the wantonness of the empty crowd: Juno, Cupid, Venus, names for self-indulgence.
opinions.original: Concordes animae casto sociantur amore, / virgo puer Christi, virgo puella dei... absit ab his thalamis vani lascivia vulgi, / Iuno Cupido Venus, nomina luxuriae.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894; OCR slips corrected)
opinions.today: Most people today enjoy lavish, festive weddings; a sober, religious-only celebration is a minority taste. Splits on how much party a wedding should have.

opinions.position: Grieve with faith: a child who dies is alive with God and can pray for his parents. He buried his own week-old son beside martyrs, trusting the saints' nearness.
opinions.side_note: Hope-filled grief, bound up with the cult of the saints.
opinions.quote: Such too was our own little one, who bore your blessed name. He was called away at the very time he was given: a child long wished for, and not granted to us, who were unworthy to rejoice in holy descendants. We believe he plays with you, Celsus, in the evergreen fields, sharing your joy and life.
opinions.original: qualis et ille fuit noster, tuus ille beati / nominis, accitus tempore quo datus est, / exoptata diu soboles nec praestita nobis / gaudere indignis posteritate pia; / credimus aeternis illum tibi, Celse, uirectis / laetitiae et uitae ludere participem
opinions.work: Carmen 31, consolation to Pneumatius and Fidelis on the death of their son Celsus
opinions.location: lines 601-606 (and 619-620: as many years as you lived, Celsus, so many days did he)
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894; OCR slips corrected)
opinions.today: Many bereaved parents today share the hope; many others find such consolation hard to accept. Splits by belief.

opinions.position: Our part is to desire God's will; accomplishing it is God's. He boasts only in the Lord.
opinions.side_note: Grace side, written in 394, before the Pelagian controversy; he was later a friend of Pelagius until warned.
opinions.quote: I do not boast that I have accomplished this: even if I might so boast, I would glory only in the Lord, whose it is to accomplish what it is our part to desire
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1 (1886), revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits as the grace-effort question always does.

opinions.position: Going to the saints' shrines is good. He went to Rome every year for the feast of Peter and Paul and filled Nola with pilgrims, where 'God is believed to be present to all'. Jerome, by contrast, wrote to him that heaven is as open from Britain as from Jerusalem.
opinions.side_note: Pro-pilgrimage side (against Jerome's Letter 58 and Gregory of Nyssa's Letter 2).
opinions.quote: There God is believed to be present to all: Felix is the glory of Christ without measure... It is a joy to see one city packed with many cities, so many swarms driven by one prayer.
opinions.original: praesens Deus omnibus illic / Creditur: immensi Felix est gloria Christi... Stipatam multis unam juvat urbibus urbem / Cernere, totque uno compulsa examina voto.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Splits: Catholics and Orthodox value pilgrimage; many Protestants and secular people see it as tourism or superstition, though walking pilgrimages (the Camino) are popular with everyone.

opinions.position: He welcomed the scorn his old friends heaped on his new life: insults taken for Christ's name are a pleasure.
opinions.side_note: Answering Ausonius's circle, who thought he had gone mad or been bewitched by his wife.
opinions.quote: I wish envy had just cause to start carping at me: insults taken for the name of Christ will please me.
opinions.original: Utinam justus me carpere livor / Incipiat, Christi sub nomine probra placebunt.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Many committed believers agree; most people prefer to avoid ridicule and keep faith private.

opinions.topic: new: a wife as partner in faith
opinions.position: His wife was not the cause of his 'madness', as his teacher hinted, but his partner in virtue.
opinions.side_note: Defending Therasia against Ausonius's jibe that she was a domineering 'Tanaquil'.
opinions.quote: So do not scold me, revered father, as if these pursuits had turned me wrong, and do not carp at me over my wife or a sickness of mind. Mine is not the anxious mind of Bellerophon, and my wife is no Tanaquil but a Lucretia.
opinions.original: Ne me igitur, venerande parens, his ut male versum / Increpites studiis, neque me vel conjuge carpas, / Vel mentis vitio: non anxia Bellerophontis / Mens est, nec Tanaquil mihi, sed Lucretia conjux.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Latin
opinions.today: Almost everyone today agrees spouses can share a calling; tells the quiz little except as colour.

sparring.with: Ausonius (his teacher; a nominal Christian poet)
sparring.over: Whether Paulinus should come back to poetry, friends and public life, and whether his wife had led him astray. An exchange of verse letters, loving on both sides and never resolved.
sparring.source: Paulinus, Carmina 10 and 11 (Ausonius's side in his Epistles)

sparring.over: Pilgrimage and the holy places: Jerome urged him not to come to Jerusalem ('Access to the courts of heaven is as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem'), gave him pointed advice on his writing, and later cooled towards him over his friendship with Rufinus and Melania. Paulinus's messenger Vigilantius became Jerome's bitter enemy.
Whether burial beside a saint profits the dead: Augustine answered Paulinus's question with a whole book, gently limiting the benefit to the living.
sparring.source: Augustine, On the Care to be Had for the Dead

sparring.over: His affection for Pelagius. They wrote in 417 that they knew he had loved Pelagius as a servant of God but did not know how he loved him now, and set out the case against Pelagius at length.
sparring.source: Augustine, Letter 186 (Latin; the file on augustinus.it is numbered 191 but holds Epistola 186)

sparring.over: His renunciation of his senatorial career and fortune, which they called unbearable.

portraits.title: San Paolino che libera lo schiavo (Saint Paulinus freeing the slave), Pio Monte della Misericordia, Naples
Saint Paulinus (icon from the Russian Lives of the Saints)
The early Christian basilica of St Felix at Cimitile, with the tombs of Felix and Paulinus (place, not portrait)
